Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Dr. M Zahir and SM Munir, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners 
Md. Khalilur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No.2. 
AF Hasan Arif, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent Nos.1 and 3

full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan J: At the instance of Ariff A. Shekha and 9 others a Rule Nisi was issued by this court on 19.7.87 calling upon the respondents to show cause why the order communicated vide Memo No. Shilpa/Dairy No. 937/DT-2/87/3028 dated 27.5.87 (Annexure-H) should not be declared to have been made and issued illegally and without lawful, authority and why direction should not be issued upon the respondents to forthwith release the Company Eastern Tubes Ltd. and its assets to the petitioners or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. Subsequently in course of hearing of the Rule on an application filed and moved by the petitioners another Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Notification bearing No. 186-81 dated 31.12.71 issued in respect of Eastern Tubes Ltd. Tejgaon Industrial Area under Group No. F (i) (8)- Tejgaon Industrial Area, published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 3rd January, 1972 (Annexure-A) to the writ petition should not be declared to have been made and published illegally and without lawful authority and why a direction should not be issued upon the respondents to withdraw/cancel/rescind the same forthwith or such other or further order or order passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 The petitioners are the share-holders of the Company, Eastern Tubes Limited, which is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 in the former East Pakistan and registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies at Dhaka on 26.6.94. The petitioners are the shareholders of the company having their respective shares and all of them together held 1,04,265 shares out of total 1,70,000 shares, and 19,240 shares are held by Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Shangsta. These constitute 72.65% of the share-holding of the said company. The company was running its industry manufacturing fluorescent tube lights at Tejgaon Industrial Area through their appointed directors, managers, officers and other executive’s at all relevant times. The Government of Bangladesh under the Acting President's Order No. SEC-X1/1M-35/71/17 dated 30.12.1971 by Notification No. 186-S1 dated 31.12.71 placed the same under the Management Board and subsequently placed it under the Engineering and Ship Building Corporation vide Notification No. P/E-1/ 1855 dated 17.5.1972 for the management of the aforesaid business. The said management also continued under Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1971 (President's Order No. 16 of 1972). The taking over of the Company and its assets was challenged by the share-holders vide letters dated 20.1.72, 15.2.72 and 4.6.72. On many occasions share-holders pressed for the release of the business of the company but the Government did not respond. The petitioner Ariff A. Shekha received letter for the first time on 22.2.78 whereby the prayer for the release of the company to the share-holders was rejected. On receipt of Mr. Ariff's letter dated 23-2-78 and 18-7-78 the Ministry asked for the documents and proof of nationality of the share-holders vide its Memo No. IND/DC-1/SSC-29 77-787 dated 21.10.78 and Memo No. IND/ DC-1/SSC-29/77-537 dated 31.8.79. Further case of the petitioner is that in the meantime Bella Artifitex Industries Limited and some other sister enterprises of the said company in which major shares were held by the same group of persons was released to the shareholders by the Government being satisfied as to genuineness of the claim of the shareholders. Suddenly the petitioner No. 1 received Memo No. Shilpa/Dairy No. 937/Dt-2/87/3028 dated 27.5.87 which was addressed to Mr. Md. Ashraf Daud, Executive Director of Bella Artifitex Industries Limited intimating that Eastern Tubes Limited and another company would not be released to its share-holders like Bella Artifitex Industries Ltd. as the Government has decided to disinvest these two industrial units by giving 51% and 49% shares of the said two companies to the Corporation and the general public respectively. On receipt of the Memo dated 27.5.87 containing the decision of the Government as regards Eastern Tubes Ltd. the petitioners sent a notice demanding justice by registered post on 21.6.87 to the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 but no reply having been received by the petitioners it is presumed that justice has been denied to them. The petitioners thereafter having moved this application before this Court obtained the instant Rule. 

 The learned Deputy Attorney-General argued that since an industrial enterprise established under Article 10(1) (a) to (d) can be placed by the Government under a Corporation it is immaterial as to whether the Company is an abandoned property or not. Once it is placed under a Corporation the vesting of its shares or other proprietory interests in the Government is complete and its abandoned character is a question of the past. It is submitted that the placing took place under the Government's general power of placement of all kinds of industrial enterprises and the resultant vesting is immune from any attack or challenge. Even if the industrial enterprise was not taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 or under President's Order 16/72 the vesting of its shares or other proprietory interests taken place for the first time under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 is not invalid unless it could be shown that the placement is prompted by any malafide intention but under such circumstances the question of payment of compensation to the former share-holders will arise. Since it is claimed that an industrial enterprise was placed under the Corporation because it was taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 then vested under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and treated as an abandoned property as such, the placement was made not because it was just an industrial enterprise left uncared for by the owners or shareholders but because it was earlier declared and treated as an abandoned property. While analysing the scope of application of Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 we have seen that Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 applies in three situations 1) where the owners, directors or managers, or the majority of them, or any industrial or commercial concern have left Bangladesh, or 2) are not available to control and manage the concern, or 3) where, in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh, the owners or directors of any industrial or commercial concern cannot be allowed, in the public interest, to control and manage the concern. To determine whether the company and its shares were placed under the Corporation under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 legally and properly, it is to be seen whether the vesting of the property as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was legal and valid. It is submitted by the Deputy Attorney- General appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 that the industrial enterprise and commercial concern were taken over and placed under the Corporation by operation of Article 4 of Nationalisation Order, 1972 and vested in the Government under its general power of placement and no such order of placement can be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise had not vested in the Government, or that the industrial enterprise was not liable to be vested in the Government. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that in the instant case the company and its assets and shares having been taken over and placed not under the general power of the authority but for the reason that it was taken over under Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71, regularised under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and then vested as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972, such taking over and placement is not immune from challenge. It has been found by the Supreme Court in the case reported in 45 DLR (AD) 69 that placement is the cause and the vesting is the result and therefore the placement of the property before it is taken over and vesting the same under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 is not proper. The basis of challenge is that the industrial enterprise on its being treated as abandoned property could not be placed under the corporation under Article 10(1) of President's Order No. 27 of 1972 and that being the basis of challenge is available to the petitioners in spite of the bar of Article 10(1A) and Article 4(1) as introduced in President's Order No. 27 of 1972 by Ordinance XXV of 1976. The question arises as to whether the company which owned the industrial enterprise was taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and declared as abandoned property and, as such, its shares and proprietory interests have vested in the Government under the Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (president's Order No. 27 of 1972) and placed under the Corporation. The company was declared as abandoned industrial unit in terms of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and thereafter the Government took over the management and control of the same. It is to be seen whether the company and its shares could be declared as abandoned property. If the application of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 is found to be unauthorized subsequent action taken on the basis of unauthorized decision were also unauthorized. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the company was incorporated in the country before 25th March, 1971 and all the share-holders, directors, managers and staffs were present at that time and hence the question of taking over of the property under Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 did not arise and furthermore, the company has not also fallen within the mischief of the definition of Article 2(1) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 which runs as follows: 

 12. Though under sub-article 2(1) (ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1) are included within the definition of the abandoned property but under Article 2(1) (i) (ii) (a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh are excluded. The question whether the property could be taken over initially under the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 was also raised in the case of Helal Jute Press Ltd. vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 551 wherein it was held: 

 13. The learned Advocate for the petitioners argued that in the present case notwithstanding the fact that the company was incorporated within the territory now comprising Bangladesh the major share-holders of the company in question themselves may not be present in the country at the relevant time but they were not engaged in war on any occasion as they were British and Malaysian nationals and two of the shareholders were Bangladeshi nationals and the managers and top executives of the company were available in Bangladesh to manage and control the company. In the case reported in 27 DLR 1551 it was further held: 

 17. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Messers ATJ Industries Ltd. and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 the question regarding the interpretation of Articles 2(2) and 4 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order was raised and it has been held that: 

 18. Thus from the principle laid down in the case cited above, it is found that the construction of Article 2(1) is implicit in the determination of a property as an abandoned property. Therefore preliminary formation of the opinion of the Government is necessary. In this connection the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Mirza Shahab lspahani reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116 may also be referred. In the said case the question of dual nationality was raised and it was contended by the Appellant-Government that the respondent cannot be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh within the meaning of the provisions of Articles 2 and 2A of the President's Order No. 149 of 1972 and, therefore, the property fell within the definition of abandoned property under Article 2(1) (i) of President's Order of 16 of 1972. The respondent contended that his property is not an abandoned property as he never ceased to look after his property after liberation in 1971 and he also made representation to the Government but the Government refused to consider the same. The Appellate Division re-iterated the earlier decision in which it was held that: 

 "The law of abandoned property is a stringent law no doubt, but as has been noticed in 28 DLR and 30 DLR (SC) the definition contains the clause on exclusion and inclusion. One thing is very well settled that no person shall be deprived of his life and property unless it comes within the clear provisions of law itself. He cannot be deprived of his property by fallacious approach nor by provisions of enactment which merely by side wind points a finger to such property. To be taken away of any property it must be shown that his property has come within the mischief of law clearly." 

 21. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel, submitted that a share-holder of a company has no direct interest in the property of the company. The learned Counsel cited the case of Punjab Ali Pramanik and others vs. Mohd, Mokarram Hossain reported in 39 DLR (SC) 185. The learned Counsel has also cited the case of EBM Company Ltd. vs. Dominion Bank reported in 1937 (PC) 279 wherein it was observed "Their Lordships were unable to support the decision in favour of the Bank upon the grounds suggested by Riddell, JA. They believe it to be of supreme importance that the distinction should be clearly marked, observed and maintained between an incorporated company's legal entity and its actions, assets, rights and liabilities on the one hand, and the individual shareholders and their actions, assets, rights, and liabilities on the other hand." 

 22. The principles laid down in the cited case are not relevant and helpful for the purpose of coming to a decision in the instant case. From the facts and circumstances and the submissions made by the learned counsels of the respective parties it is found that this company along with its assets and shares was first taken over under Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971 then regularized under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and with the promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the company along with its shares and assets were treated as abandoned property on the alleged ground that the shareholders and the officers were not found available in Bangladesh to take control and management of the company. At the time of taking over the company as abandoned the formation of the opinion of the Government as to its abandoned character was necessary. It is submitted by Mr. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2, that the shares of the company Artifitex Ltd. were not released but sold to the previous share-holders. Under sub-clause (a) of clause (i) of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the property of the person who is away from the country for a temporary period being not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh and under sub-clause (b) of the said Article 2(1) (ii) of President's Order No; 16 of 1972 the property or industrial concern though taken over under the possession and control of the Government under the Action President's Order No. 1 of 1972 are excluded from being declared and treated as abandoned property. Furthermore, before declaring a company as abandoned Government is to form opinion that the owners and share-holders were absent from the country and were not found to control and manage the company and or that they were residing in a country which was at war or engaged in military operation with Bangladesh after 25th day of March, 1971 . This view gets support from the case reported in 30 DLR (SC) 101 and 40 DLR (AD) 116. The control and management of the enterprises in question having been taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 it falls within the exclusive clause of Article 2 of President Order No. 16 of 1972 and, therefore, we are of the view that the vesting of the company and shares thereof bringing it within the mischief of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and on that ground placing and vesting of the same to the corporation under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 by the Government without applying its mind so as to hold that the absence of the share-holders were prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh, cannot be accepted. As the definition of the abandoned property were not attracted in the instant case, the company and all its assets could not be said to have vested in the Government and consequently the taking over of the company along with its assets and shares and placing the same for the management and control of the Corporation on the ground that it was treated as abandoned cannot also be said to have been validly done. In the instant case separate Rule was issued on the prayer of the petitioners by this court on 23.1.91 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the notification bearing No.186-SI dated 31.12.71 in respect of the company and subsequently regularized by the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1971 published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary of January, 3, 1972 should not be declared to have been made and published illegally and without lawful authority. From the notification it appears that the company was taken over along with all its property's assets located in Bangladesh for appointing management board to operate and conduct the affairs of the enterprise. This is not a case that under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 the industrial enterprise were taken over and vested in the Government applying Articles 4 and 10(1A) regardless and also independent of the vesting of the property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Had it been so then it would have been necessary for us to see whether the placement of the company and its share thereof under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was lawful or not As the company and its shares have been vested under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 on the ground that it was vested in the Government as abandoned property, under President's Order 16 of 1972 if it is found. that the company and shares thereof does not carry abandoned character then the shares of the petitioners who were found to have been away from the country and have been residing as its national in any country which was not at war with Bangladesh could not be treated as abandoned shares and for that matter could remain vested with the Government. Furthermore, it will not be out of place here to mention that the Ministry of Industries acknowledged the share certificates submitted by the petitioners for the purpose of compensation in respect of Eastern Tubes Limited and Annexure-X series to the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioners and Annexure-J filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 along with the affidavit- in-reply filed by the petitioners and the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent Nos. 1-3 show the share-holding position of the petitioners in company in question and contain the statements of verification of shares by the Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation for the purpose of payment of compensation to the share-holders of Eastern Tubes Limited.
